en_alt: The children rush into the water.
The children throw themselves into the water.
note: "Fling themselves" is fine but the headword gloss is "to rush" and «броса́ться» is literally "throw oneself"; both alternatives should be accepted.

ru: Ле́том мы броса́лись в ре́ку ка́ждый день.
en: In summer we used to rush into the river every day.
note: Imperfective past plus «ка́ждый день» is habitual; "used to rush" commits to that and de-collides with the perfective partners' plain "rushed".

ru: Он всегда́ броса́ется на по́мощь дру́гу.
В жару́ де́ти бу́дут броса́ться в во́ду.
Она́ бро́сила кури́ть в про́шлом году́.
en_alt: She quit smoking last year.
She stopped smoking last year.
note: «Бро́сить кури́ть» has several equally standard English renderings; the word-bank drill should accept them.

ru: Е́сли бы я мог, я бы бро́сил кури́ть сра́зу.
en_alt: If I could, I would quit smoking straight away.
note: Equally valid rendering of «бро́сил кури́ть сра́зу».

en_alt: Tomorrow he will give up the old habit.
note: The Russian has no possessive; "the old habit" is the literal reading and should also be accepted.

en_alt: Will you quit smoking?
note: Equally standard rendering.

en_alt: I will throw you the ball.
note: Both English orders are natural for the dative.

ru: Е́сли бы бы́ло ну́жно, я бы бро́силась в во́ду.
Е́сли бу́дет ну́жно, я бы бро́силась в во́ду.
ru_new: Е́сли бу́дет ну́жно, я бро́шусь в во́ду.
en: If it is necessary, I will rush into the water.
note: A future-indicative protasis «Е́сли бу́дет ну́жно» cannot govern a бы-conditional apodosis; the sentence must be either fully conditional (which would duplicate the sibling «Е́сли бы бы́ло ну́жно…») or fully future, as here.

en: The children broke into a run.
en_alt: The children rushed off running.
note: "Rushed to run" is not English; «бро́ситься бежа́ть» is to break into a run / take off running.

ru: Тепе́рь мы бу́дем быва́ть у ба́бушки ча́ще.
en_alt: Now we will visit grandmother more often.
note: «Ба́бушка» is glossed "grandmother"; both forms should be accepted.

ru: Он быва́л в Москве́ мно́го раз.
en_alt: He has visited Moscow many times.
note: Matches the headword gloss as well as the idiomatic "has been to".

The English is right, but this is the existential sense of «быва́ть» ("there are, from time to time"), which the headword gloss "to visit sometimes" does not cover — the gloss may be the half that needs widening.

ru: Без дел я быва́л бы там ка́ждый день.
en_alt: With nothing to do I would be there every day.
note: "Visit there" is marginal English; the natural reading of «быва́л бы там» is "would be there".

en_alt: Be at home by dinner.
note: Both are natural for «до́ма».

en_alt: Perhaps it will rain tomorrow.
Maybe there will be rain tomorrow.
note: «Бу́дет дождь» is literally "there will be rain"; both readings are correct.

en_alt: Tomorrow I will be home.
note: Equally natural rendering of «до́ма».

ru: Без тебя́ ве́чер был бы ску́чным.
en_alt: Without you the evening would be boring.
note: «Ску́чный» is glossed "boring"; both should be accepted.

ru: Е́сли бы я был бога́т, я бы путеше́ствовал.
Без ве́тра снег не вали́л бы так гу́сто.
note: The English is correct, but «вали́ть» of snow means to come down thickly, a sense the headword gloss "to topple" does not cover.

en: The workers were pulling down the old shed.
en_alt: The workers were demolishing the old shed.
note: You fell trees, not sheds; "felling the old shed" is not English.

ru: За́втра рабо́чие бу́дут вали́ть ста́рые дере́вья.
Без дел кот валя́лся бы на со́лнце весь день.

en_alt: The cat is lying around on the sofa.
The cat is sprawled on the sofa.
note: "Lounging" is good but the headword gloss is "to lie around"; both should be accepted.

ru: В воскресе́нье я бу́ду валя́ться в посте́ли до полу́дня.
Я валя́юсь в посте́ли по утра́м.

en_alt: Cook the soup over a low heat.
Simmer the soup over a low heat.
note: "Over a low heat" is the standard British collocation for «на ме́дленном огне́».

en_alt: I brew coffee every morning.
note: «Вари́ть ко́фе» is standardly "brew coffee" as well as "make coffee".

en_alt: Grandmother made jam in the summer.
note: The imperfective past also supports a plain past reading.

ru: Без реце́пта я бы вари́л суп по-сво́ему.

en_alt: Do you make jam in the summer?
note: Article choice on «ле́том» is free in English.

ru: Учи́тель ввёл нас в курс де́ла.
en_alt: The teacher brought us up to date with the matter.
The teacher put us in the picture.
note: «Ввести́ в курс де́ла» is idiomatic; a less opaque rendering alongside it teaches the structure.

ru: Е́сли бы реши́ли на собра́нии, ввели́ бы но́вый поря́док.
en_alt: If it were decided at the meeting, they would introduce a new order.
note: «Поря́док» is glossed "order"; both renderings are correct here.

en_alt: The train was taking passengers to the south.
note: Matches the headword gloss "to be taking" as well as "carrying".

ru: За́втра он бу́дет везти́ това́р на ры́нок.
Без маши́ны я бы везла́ э́то на теле́жке.
en_alt: Without a car I would be taking this in a cart.
note: Both prepositions are natural for «на теле́жке».

en_alt: Mother told the children to be quiet.
The mother ordered the children to keep quiet.
note: «Веле́ть» spans "order" and "tell"; anarthrous "Mother" is equally natural.

ru: На его́ ме́сте я бы веле́л всем замолча́ть.
en_alt: In his place I would order everyone to fall silent.
note: «Замолча́ть» is glossed "to fall silent"; the more literal reading should also be accepted.

ru: За́втра врач бу́дет веле́ть ему́ отдыха́ть.
По́сле тако́й лжи ты бы ему́ ве́рил?
en_alt: After such a lie would you believe him?
note: Russian fronts the adverbial; the matching English order is equally natural and should be accepted.

ru: Без доказа́тельств я не бу́ду ве́рить слуха́м.

note: The imperfective English is right, but the perfective partner «Она́ пове́рила в успе́х.» is also just "believed in success" — the perfective side should read "came to believe", so the fix belongs there, not here.

ru: Е́сли бы я мог, я бы верну́л э́ти дни.

en_alt: Return the keys to their place!
Put the keys back where they belong!
note: Several equally natural renderings of «на ме́сто».

en_alt: He gave me back the money.
note: Equally natural rendering of «верну́л мне».

en: Soon he will repay the debt.
en_alt: Soon he will pay back the debt.
note: English does not "return a debt"; «верну́ть долг» is to repay/pay back a debt.

en_alt: Come back before nine o'clock.
Be back before nine o'clock.
note: «До» is literally "before"; both readings are natural.

en_alt: When will you return?
note: Matches the headword gloss as well as "come back".

ru: Е́сли бы не дождь, мы бы верну́лись ра́ньше.

en_alt: We will come back to this question.
note: Equally natural rendering.

en_alt: I will definitely return here in summer.
note: Article on «ле́том» is free in English.

en_alt: Will you come back in an hour?
note: Equally natural rendering.

en_alt: I will come back in an hour.
note: Equally natural rendering.

en: How are you enjoying yourselves at the party?
en_alt: How do you have fun at a celebration?
note: "How are you having fun" is not idiomatic English; the natural rendering of «как вы весели́тесь» is "how are you enjoying yourselves".

en_alt: The children are enjoying themselves at the party.
note: Equally natural rendering of «веселя́тся».

en_alt: Yesterday we had great fun.
note: Equally natural rendering of «о́чень весели́лись».

en_alt: With friends I always have fun.
note: The Russian fronts «с друзья́ми»; the matching English order is equally natural.

ru: По́сле о́тпуска чемода́н бу́дет ве́сить бо́льше.
Без воды́ посы́лка ве́сила бы ме́ньше.
en_alt: Without water the parcel would weigh less.
note: Russian has no article; the anarthrous reading is equally valid.

ru: Без тебя́ я бы вёл соба́ку оди́н.
en_alt: Without you I would be walking the dog on my own.
note: «Оди́н» reads equally as "alone" or "on my own".

en_alt: Are you leading the children to school?
note: Matches the headword gloss "to be leading" as well as the idiomatic "taking".

en_alt: The teacher is taking the children to the museum.
note: Equally natural rendering of «ведёт».

ru: За́втра гид бу́дет вести́ нас по го́роду.
en_alt: Tomorrow the guide will be leading us around the town.
note: «Го́род» reads as either "city" or "town".

ru: Я взгляну́ на докуме́нты ещё раз за́втра.
en_alt: I will glance at the documents again tomorrow.
note: «Ещё раз» is equally "again" or "once more".

ru: Е́сли бы я знал, я бы взгляну́л внима́тельнее.

en_alt: I will glance at this picture.
note: Matches the headword gloss "to glance" as well as "take a look".

en_alt: Take a look at the sky!
Have a look at the sky!
note: Bare "Glance at…" is a marginal English imperative; the periphrastic forms are what a speaker would actually say.

en_alt: She glanced at her watch.
note: «Часы́» is clock or watch; both readings are correct here.

en_alt: Will you glance at your watch?
note: «Часы́» is clock or watch; both readings are correct here.

ru: По́сле экза́мена я наконе́ц вздохну́ споко́йно.
en_alt: After the exam I will finally breathe easy.
note: «Вздохну́ть споко́йно» is standardly "breathe easy"; both renderings are correct.

en_alt: She sighed deeply.
note: «Глубоко́ вздохну́ла» reads as either a deep breath or a deep sigh; the gloss is "to sigh".

en_alt: Will you be able to breathe easy?
note: Same idiom as the sibling sentence; both renderings should be accepted.

ru: На его́ ме́сте я бы то́лько вздохну́ла.

en_alt: You will shudder at such a sound.
note: The headword gloss and the sibling sentences use "shudder"; it should be accepted here too.

en_alt: She flinched in fright.
note: "Flinched from fright" is not an English collocation, and "shudder" matches the headword gloss and the sibling sentences.

en_alt: She will shudder at a loud sound.
note: The unfronted English order is equally natural.

ru: Е́сли бы дверь хло́пнула, я бы вздро́гнул.

en_alt: She took the bag and left.
note: The Russian has no possessive; the anarthrous reading should also be accepted.

ru: Е́сли бы шёл дождь, я бы взял зо́нтик.

en_alt: The book was borrowed from the library.
note: «Взять в библиоте́ке» is specifically to borrow; both readings teach something.

ru: Без де́нег я бы не взяла́ такси́.
Он взя́лся за рабо́ту с утра́.
en_alt: He set to work in the morning.
He got down to work first thing in the morning.
note: «С утра́» is literally "from the morning"; several renderings are equally natural.

ru: Е́сли бы бы́ло вре́мя, я бы взя́лся за рабо́ту сейча́с.

en_alt: Where did this money appear from?
note: «Взя́ться» here means to appear/turn up, a sense the gloss "to take hold of" does not cover; the alt makes that reading available.

ru: Ско́ро он возьмётся за учёбу всерьёз.
en_alt: Soon he will get down to his studies seriously.
note: «Учёба» reads as either "studying" or "studies".

en_alt: Will you take on the work?
note: «Взя́ться за рабо́ту» is equally "take on the work".

en_alt: We have not seen such wonders.
note: The Russian has plain negation without «никогда́»; the alt drops the added "never" and expands the negation for the word bank.

en_alt: I have not seen him for a long time.
note: «Давно́» is glossed "long ago"; the uncontracted, more literal form should also be accepted.

«Вида́ть» is barely used in the present tense — a speaker would say «Ты ви́дишь э́ту го́ру отсю́да?»; the same applies to the sibling «бу́дешь вида́ть», so this looks like a paradigm-generation artefact rather than a translation defect.

ru: В таку́ю пого́ду ты бу́дешь вида́ть го́ры отсю́да.
Без очко́в я бы не вида́л доро́гу.

en_alt: Do you see this picture?
note: «Карти́на» is glossed "picture" corpus-wide; that reading should be accepted here.

ru: С балко́на ты бу́дешь ви́деть всё мо́ре.

en_alt: Do you see the road?
note: The Russian has no modal; the literal reading should also be accepted.

ru: Без очко́в я бы не ви́дела э́тих букв.
